title: Design, drawings & BOQ
headline: Decide exactly what you are building — and what it should cost — before anyone mixes concrete.
seoTitle: House design, structural drawings and Bill of Quantities (BOQ) in Nigeria explained
seoDescription: What architectural, structural and services drawings you need, how a Bill of Quantities works, and how to use it to control your contractor in Nigeria.
summary: Good drawings and a proper Bill of Quantities (BOQ) are your contract with the builder. Without them, every change becomes a negotiation.
duration: 4–10 weeks for design and drawings; 1–3 weeks for a BOQ, depending on size [CHECK]
whatHappens: Architectural drawings: floor plans, elevations, sections and a site plan showing setbacks. These show rooms, sizes, doors, windows and heights.

Structural drawings by a registered engineer (COREN): foundation type, column and beam sizes, slab details and reinforcement (rod sizes and spacing). Needed for any storey building and strongly advised for bungalows.
Services drawings: plumbing, drainage, septic/soak-away, and electrical layouts (sockets, lights, DB board, earthing).

Bill of Quantities (BOQ): a quantity surveyor measures every item from the drawings (m³ of concrete, m² of blockwork, tonnes of rods, number of doors…) and prices it. It lets you compare contractors line by line and pay for work actually done.
Specification: what grade of materials — block size and strength, cement brand, concrete mix, roofing gauge, tile quality, sanitary fittings.
Programme: the order and expected duration of the stages, which becomes the basis for staged payments.
problems: Building from a ‘sketch’ only. Sizes change on site, rooms shrink and costs grow.
No structural design — columns and beams sized ‘by experience’. This is how buildings crack or collapse.
A quotation that is one lump sum with no quantities. You cannot check it or compare it.
BOQ quantities inflated (more concrete, rods or blocks than the drawings need), or prices hidden in ‘sundries’ and ‘provisional sums’.
Cheap specification slipped in: 6-inch blocks where 9-inch were drawn, thinner roofing sheets, lower-grade rods.
Design changes made by phone with no written variation and price — the final bill becomes a surprise.
questions: Who prepared the architectural and structural drawings, and are they registered (ARCON / COREN)?
Can I have the BOQ with quantities and rates for every item, not just a total?
Which items are ‘provisional sums’ or ‘prime cost sums’, and how will they be adjusted?
What is the specification for blocks, concrete mix, reinforcement, roofing and finishes?
What is the programme, and how do payments line up with completed stages?
How will changes be agreed and priced before they are done?
photoCheckpoints: PDF copies of all drawings with the professionals’ names, seals and dates.
The full BOQ in Excel or PDF with quantities, units and rates.
A one-page specification sheet you have signed off.
The agreed payment schedule tied to stages.
